Taken to its ultimate conclusions, it leads to a place where we don’t wish to follow: the dead end that is nihilism. The relationship that the LH brings via the scientific method and its implied materialism, is not a non-existence of a relationship of us and the world, but rather a disengaged one that implies, incorrectly, observers having no impact on the observed, as well as there being no altering effect on the observing person caused by what the person observes and how. The “betweenness” we encountered before is not absent, just denied.
Whatever denial is employed, the fact remains that how we attend to the world changes not just other things and people, but also who we are. We must be conscious of what we spend our time attending to — and how.
“False Friends” of the Hemispheres Two words in different languages that may look or sound similar but carry a completely different meaning are often referred to as “false friends”. There are a few common words, whose meaning and interpretation differs substantially depending on which hemisphere explains them. Some of the more illustrative ones covered in the book are the following.
Belief. For the LH, belief is laced with uncertainty, doubt, or outright falsity, making it a lesser form of the certain knowing and thinking that defines its mode of operation. For the RH, belief is a matter of caring and having a relationship with someone or something. For example, the statements “I believe in you” or “I believe in God” are not, as espoused by the RH, implying that one thinks or knows something with a degree of uncertainty, but rather reflect having an attitude towards something, a certain disposition towards an aspect of the world. With it come characteristic behaviours and responsibilities.
Will. Willing shares properties with believing, in that it is connected to having a certain disposition towards the world. For the LH it is one of use and control, but for the RH, with its open and caring disposition that values relationships, will relates to a desire or longing towards something, towards “Other”.
Familiarity. The LH sees generic and general things to be familiar, those things that have constantly been re-presented by it and have thus been ontologically demoted and emptied of meaning. Essentially the opposite is the case for the RH, which sees those parts of the world as familiar that are constantly present, but have thus been enriched over time with meaning.
Newness. Related to the above, newness, for the RH, is perhaps best described as a seeing for the first time what seems only too familiar through a patient openness that cannot be willed. Contrarily, the sense of novelty for the LH is constructed at will via the recombination of already known elements, such that the resulting distance from the familiar, uniqueness, and bizarreness shocks us into novelty.
Activity & Passivity. Loss of control and loss of self-determination is seen as passivity from the perspective of the LH. Consequently, only a restoration thereof means that you are active. But it is exactly this passivity that the RH endorses, this patient openness as required for newness, enabling things to come to you less by what is done and more by what is not done. The RH sees activity in the not doing part, which makes it able to experience both activity and passivity in the same process or experience, a feat that is denied to the LH with its “either/or” thinking.
The Primacy of the Right Hemisphere Neurophysiological evidence clearly indicated the RH to have precedence over the LH. The RH underwrites all knowledge the LH comes to have, as it alone is the first point of contact with experience and decides what information gets passed along. The Primacy of the RH is further evidenced by the fact that it alone is capable of synthesising the fragments of knowledge from both hemispheres into a usable whole.
Besides visible in scientific evidence, the order of exchange between the hemispheres is mirrored in many other processes as well, in various domains and on various scales. Foreshadowing the contents and analysis of the second part of the book, Iain explains that we can see a similarity of the cycle of philosophy to the way information is cycled through the hemispheres: What started as a sense of awe, wonder, and curiosity as lived through the RH progressed through inspections from a dizzying amount of angles using the mechanistic logic and language of the LH, which were gradually synthesised because of the realisation that language, linearity, and certainty must themselves be transcended with the help of the RH, ending in the painstakingly regained profound sense of wonder of the 20th century.
This and other similar analyses have a common theme underlying them all, again reflecting the primacy of the RH: Metaphor, as subserved by the RH, comes before denotation, as subserved by the LH. It is a historical truth, as well as an epistemological fact, as one cannot draw something away and make it abstract (Latin: abs-, away, and trahere, pull) unless there is already something to draw it away from. In other words, one cannot unfold something and make it explicit (Latin: ex-, out, and plicare, fold) unless it is already folded. We experience many things being implicit in their nature. Making them explicit, as we do via language, changes their nature. Too much of this explicitness, too much self-awareness, and we destroy meaning until things become mechanical and lifeless.
Only the frame of mind of the RH makes certain things possible, such as going to sleep, entering a flow state, or cultivating and exhibiting wisdom. Importantly, the RH allows for a “semi-opaque” view, where we rest our attention on the object while retaining awareness of the depth given by its contextual and environmental embedding. The spotlight vision of the LH effectively projects things onto a plane and transforms it into abstract shapes in the process. It does so in an attempt to see something “clearly”, such that we can exercise control. However, it is precisely this partial transparency that makes us see a painting neither as an amalgam of colored patches nor as a mere window, but as a layer through which we can optimally grasp reality, while being part of it.
Before Cognition An inevitable component to include in discussions about awareness, decisions, and our conscious processing thereof is the work of Benjamin Libet in 1985 (and earlier work by Hans Kornhuber). The work showed that the urge to follow through with the action of one’s choosing is only seen in the neurophysiological data about 0.2 seconds after the so called “readiness potential”, which roughly measures motor cortex activity that leads to muscle movement. In a way, the mind knew that its owner was going to decide to act before carrying out the action. Naturally, the findings spawned a myriad of intellectual debates about free will. It is mentioned in the book partly because Iain expresses his opinion, that this work only becomes an issue when believing solely the conscious parts of the mind to constitute the “me”, a notion he does not endorse. In a world after the works of Freud, Jung, and others about the vastness of our subconscious, it is even perplexing that such limiting views of the self are still held by many.
Another landmark study, which is more closely related to the two worlds of the hemispheres, is that of David McNeill on gestures and speech. It revealed that thought originates in the RH with a “largely imagistic and minimally analytic” nature, focusing on the Gestalt and holistic description of the thought content, which is gesticular in nature. Only afterwards does the LH get involved by providing a linguistic structure with which to integrate these thoughts, and by the moment of utterance there is a synthesis of both holistic and analytic cognitive functions as provided by the RH and LH, respectively. A particularly striking finding concerns the situation where and when there is a mismatch between gesture and speech: it is always the gesture that carries the meaning of the thought correctly to its conclusions when there is a verbal mistake. Iain concludes that “The evidence from McNeill’s work is that — temporally, logically and ontologically — the right-hemisphere world grounds that of the left.”
That the implicit grounds the explicit is also supported by research that shows us to first make an intuitive assessment of the whole before any cognitive processes come into play, though they will be used later to explain and justify our choices. That such emotional reactions and feelings precede full cognitive processing — affect coming first, thinking later — is referred to as the primacy of affect. It is made sense of by further evidence suggesting that perceptual-cognitive awareness appears to have developed on the back of (or, anatomically speaking, on top of) affective awareness that served as a “revolutionary prerequisite” in the words of the neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp, and he further writes that the sentiment of Descartes “I think, therefore I am” may be actually superseded by “I feel, therefore I am”. Emotion and the body are the irreducible core of experience, reason emanating from it to give us the ability to limit and direct emotions, so much so that the French philosopher Vauvenargues has said “emotion has taught mankind to reason”. Even the prejudice we have in favour of reason cannot itself be justified by reasoning — we intuit the virtues of reason.
These studies and others enriched our understanding in the temporal aspects of our awareness and cognition, and showed that the processes and contents of the RH and LH are not, in a way, synchronized with each other. Interestingly, the resulting small windows during the various communications between areas in the brain allows the hemispheres to either not permit or permit aspects of being to be presented (re-presented for the LH) by saying no or not saying no, respectively. The hemispheres are apophatic and inhibitory in nature, which is reflected in the functional anatomy of the brain, specifically in the most highly evolved part of the brain, the frontal cortex. It achieves what it does by (not) negating other brain activity. Another piece to address potential restrictions about free will as raised by Libet’s experiments is the fact that there is time between unconscious initiation and conscious execution, such that we have time to intervene and “veto” the action. In this sense we may possess “free won’t” rather than free will.
Limitations of the System As explained above, it is vital that the divided and broken down world of the LH must eventually be returned to the unifying worldview of the RH, just as Hegel’s thesis and anti-thesis are supposed to be brought together to form a “syn-thesis” at a higher level. This necessity is connected to the theorems and their implications of the mathematician Kurt Gödel, when one recognises that the models created and employed by the LH resemble axiomatic systems. Loosely speaking, Gödel showed that there will always be statements that can arise from within a system whose truth the system itself cannot ascertain. What this means for the LH is that its rational means of pursuit can be impotent when it comes to achieving some of its own rationally conceived goals. It exposes the limits of the system and points beyond, in this case to the RH. It is perhaps akin to another one of Hegel’s terms, namely Aufhebung (“sublation” in English). It denotes a way in which later stages of an “organic” process are lifted up and transformed while imbuing meaning to earlier stages that may have even been incompatible or inconsistent with one another. In Hegel’s words then, the results of the LH are aufgehoben by the RH, such that they are not completely dismissed, but not taken literally either.
The systems that are created and seen as complete by the LH are, not just by the standards of the RH, but even in its own terms, incomplete. “Whether or not the superstructure holds up,” remarks Iain, “their [the systems’] foundations lie in, and are ‘bootstrapped’ on, intuition: the premises from which the rational system building begins, and even the rational mode of operation itself, that of the value of reason, cannot be confirmed by the process of rationalistic systematisation, but need ultimately to be intuited.” This perfectly captures the dilemma of the LH, which ultimately forces it to pass the scepter back to the RH.
The Relationship of the Hemispheres at Three Levels The last overarching topic of the first part of the book, and therefore for the remainder of this article, is that of the relationship the hemispheres have with one another. Their interaction is analysed on three different levels: the neurological, the phenomenological, and the last being perhaps best put as the axiological level, which consists of a number of asymmetries of different kinds.
Level One On the automatic, moment-to-moment, responsive level, on which decisions are made in milliseconds, the hemispheres are rather in opposition than collaboration. Here, once a hemisphere assumes control of a certain task — a decision based on a set of expectations concerning the nature of the task — it remains in control even if the other hemisphere would be better suited to the task and give better performance. This step happens before any actual rigorous information processing, and likely evolved as an inferior but quick solution, which is better than an inefficient back and forth information transfer across the hemispheres that delays a pressing, or perhaps even vital answer. The whole process is inhibitory in nature.
Level Two On the phenomenological level, where hemispheric interactions bring our world of experience into being, there are no neurological correlates to be measured, but rather deductions are made from what we know of the nature and typical modes of operations of each hemisphere. Since it is in the best interest of both hemispheres to deliver an interpretation of the world that promotes survival, at this higher level cooperation is required. Through repeatable results and reproducible data in experiments and studies where the hemispheres are isolated, the active regions within each hemisphere for different types of tasks have become predictable by neuroscience. However, and this was a major finding, this is not true when both hemispheres work together. The activity patterns, as well as the nature of processing cannot be predicted from what we know of the parts, as there are emergent properties, patterns, and functions. Another intriguing observation that arises at this level is that of “hemispheric utilisation bias”, which makes one hemisphere predominate, either overall or for particular kinds of experience, the bias being stronger if the LH has predominance. Despite all this, we seem to experience a single unified field of consciousness. Why this is so is a fascinating question that remains open until this day.
Level Three The last level is characterised by two asymmetries that indicate where the power ought to lie, namely with the RH, as well as three asymmetries that, however, skew the power balance in favour of the LH.
First, there is the ontological asymmetry, which exists due to the RH being the mediator of experience from which the world of the LH is derived from, and therefore depends on. Second, there is an asymmetry of function, where the products of the LH must be returned to the RH in order to make sense and to live on within something new. Although the transfer of content from the RH to the unpacking, dismantling, and analysing processes of the LH can enrich experience and further our understanding, it is not literally vital as the reverse process is. Both these asymmetries together undeniably indicate that the RH ought to be the Master and the LH his Emissary.
What makes the worldview of the LH more accessible is its proximity to our self-awareness, self-inspecting intellect. The views of the LH are more readily defensible and expressible via language and logic that are mostly controlled by it. The LH thus benefits more from an inherent asymmetry of means. Over time, the systems built by the LH also give solidity and permanence to its worldview, enabling easy transfer of knowledge that the RH with its complex, ever-changing, and holistic information cannot do. The self-referential and closed nature of these systems reflect an asymmetry of structure, treating anything not expressible via language or logic as irrelevant. Finally, the transfer process between the hemispheres favors the LH in an asymmetry of interaction. The unfolding and analysis that the LH performs to build its systems can get dragged out and further substantiated internally via the systems already built, effectively creating a positive feedback loop. As one will see in part two of the book, this substantiation of the last asymmetry can even happen externally in the corporeal world that we have learned to control and manipulate to an enormous degree.
Final Remarks The first part of the book “The Master and his Emissary” is an intellectual and literary tour de force that demonstrates the powerful lens on reality and ourselves provided by the knowledge that the hemispheres have accumulated about themselves.
What started out as an anatomical and neurophysiological ensemble of facts was woven together into a tapestry that depicts a new look on how we engage with the world and why. Whether one adopts a metaphysics more towards the side of materialism or one in the direction of idealism (or any other), it seems unavoidable to address the questions raised when studying the brain — the vehicle, facilitator, conjurer, or conduit of thought, consciousness, and our existence. Therefore, the contents of the book will be invaluable to any who seek answers, to those who want to understand reality more deeply.
I hope the article has provided the reader with enthusiasm to go read, in fact more like study, the book, a wholehearted recommendation of mine. Not only do you tremendously expand your knowledge and understanding of the brain, but you may see your thoughts, decisions, and actions in a new way — one that hopefully provides you with new means of personal evolution.
summary: This article is about part one of the book The Master and His Emissary (2009) by Iain McGilchrist. In part one, Iain gives us a comprehensive overview of the anatomy of our brain, what cognitive functions and abilities are associated with which hemisphere, and how the hemispheres each see and interact with the self and the world, and how they provide the foundations for our subjective experience. Due to their frequent use, “right hemisphere” is abbreviated as RH and “left hemisphere” as LH.
title: The Master and His Emissary by Iain McGilchrist: Part 1

contents:
This article is about part 3 of the anthology Philosophy of Science: Central Issues (1998). This part revolves around the principle of underdetermination, and the related formulations of influential philosophers such as Pierre Duhem and Willard V. O. Quine. In short, underdetermination embodies the idea, that a given body of evidence cannot uniquely determine which theories and beliefs we should espouse. This idea was already mentioned in the previous article about part 2, but will be thoroughly explained in this article.
What Experiments Can and Cannot Do. When studying the scientific literature, especially textbooks of a certain subject, we may encounter the idea of a “critical” or “crucial” experiment. An experiment that, in one stroke of demonstration, supposedly decides between two contender theories in an unequivocal manner, validating only one while invalidating the other. The clean and certain nature of such experiments appeal to our naive beliefs we may, at the initial exposures of our psyche to science and the philosophy thereof, hold with regard to such topics. The previous articles so far hopefully completely disabused the reader of such notions in the theoretical and methodological aspects of science, and this article aims to do the same with regard to the experimental side.
An apt example of such a “crucial” experiment would be the measurements of the speed of light in air and water by Léon Foucault in 1853 as part of his dissertation. Around that time, one theory that explained the refraction of light in a medium (such as water) was the corpuscular theory of light as formulated by Newton through his work in optics, wherein light was made of small particles called “corpuscles”. The only thing of importance of this theory for us here, is that it predicted light to have a larger velocity in water than in air, whereas the newly emerging wave theories of light predicted the opposite. A perfect situation for a crucial experiment. The last sentence of Foucault’s thesis1 captures the conclusion of his work succinctly:
“La conclusion dernière de ce travail consiste donc à déclarer le systeme de l’émission incompatible avec la réalité des faits.”
It translates to “The final conclusion of this work consists thus in declaring the emission system incompatible with the reality of the facts.” Emission system here means the corpuscular theory of light. Importantly for us, the whole theory was, with one experiment, seen as invalidated.
A century later, Pierre Duhem in his Physical Theory and Experiment (1954) (chapter VI of linked work) shows the impossibility of such a grand conclusion. Duhem starts by explaining that every theory is a bundle of hypotheses. To test and attempt to refute a single one via experiments is impossible, as it is always connected to an ensemble of auxiliary hypotheses. For example, Newton’s universal law of gravitation relies upon many, one may say hidden, assumptions and auxiliary statements such as the conservation of mass, the perennial magnitude of his gravitational constant, the theories allowing for the interpretation of the planetary data gathered by the measurement devices like telescopes and clocks, and so on. It would be an enormous task to list them all, if that is at all possible.
The only thing an observation or experiment can then put into question is the whole bundle of hypotheses, showing that all together may be in jeopardy. The arrow of modus tollens is simply incapable of pinpointing the erroneous piece. In other words, there is ambiguity in the falsification provided by observations. Using formal logical notation and labeling the single hypothesis (or theory), an observation, and auxiliary hypotheses with $T, O$ and $A$, respectively, we can show Duhem’s idea that a single hypothesis cannot alone predict anything as:
$$D1 \quad \sim (T \rightarrow O_1) \, , \, {\rm but \, rather}$$ $$D2 \quad (T \,\&\, A_1 \,\&\, ... \,\&\, A_n) \rightarrow O_1 \, .$$ From these, Duhem's thesis about the ambiguity of falsification logically follows: $$D3 \quad \sim (\sim O_1 \rightarrow \, \sim T) \, , \, {\rm but \, instead}$$ $$D4 \quad \sim O_1 \rightarrow \, \sim (T \,\&\, A_1 \,\&\, ... \,\&\, A_n) \, .$$ In other words, not observing the prediction ($\sim O_1$) can only criticise an intricately woven together hypothesis bundle. Foucault's experiment only criticised the portion of statements of corpuscular theory that entailed the light velocity to be higher in the medium, never the whole theory that also predicted some other phenomena quite adequately. Duhem compares this situation to mathematics, showing that in physics the theories $T$ and $\sim T$ are not logically exhaustive like in mathematics, where showing the truth of one is to disprove the other. In physics, the alternative to a theory $T$ is not $\sim T$ but rather some of the many possible rival theories $T^*$, such that we have his final statement formalised as:
$$D5 \quad \sim (\sim T \rightarrow T^*) \, .$$ It is not the case, that providing strong evidence against one theory is to validate a rival hypothesis. His work was timely, as around his time Henri Poincaré and others advocated the doctrine of conventionalism, which states that many fundamental postulates of physics are definitions adopted by convention, and as such cannot be refuted by any experiment or observation. For example, Newton’s first law, when taken in isolation, cannot be compared with experience and tested in experiments in a direct manner, so the claim. Duhem did not believe in this, using his holist thesis to argue, that although one cannot in principle refute individual hypotheses, experiments can put a whole system of hypotheses (a physical theory) into question and thereby also the individual hypothesis. The acceptance of a rival theory then, in a way, refutes the old postulates (albeit indirectly). As we can see now, history shows that he was right, in a way, as relativity theory overthrew (in certain regimes and on certain scales) Newtonian mechanics, effectively refuting “definitions” within it.
The only lurking problem in all of this, is that you could use these arguments to forever cling to your favorite theory, always providing yet another auxiliary hypothesis to mend and save the theory if evidence grows against it. For this, Duhem only appealed to what he called “good sense” (or common sense), which makes one abandon a theory eventually. Below we will see another philosopher enlighten us on this issue.
The Reach of Refutations A similar but stronger idea was given by W. V. O. Quine in his Two Dogmas of Empiricism (1953), where he argues that an attempt at refutation of a single statement actually affects the complete contemporary body of scientific knowledge. Quine saw science as a man-made field whose boundary conditions are experiences. All statements are logically interconnected and none is immune to revision if there’s conflict with experience. His arguments rely on a sophisticated understanding of analytic and synthetic statements, whose explanations go beyond the scope of this article. Suffice it to say, what he saw as being criticised by observation and experiment, which he called “The unit of empirical significance”, he believed “is the whole of science”.
To extend the scope to this ultimate limit was deemed untenable by Donald Gillies when he wrote The Duhem Thesis and the Quine Thesis (1993) (chapter 5 of the linked work). In short, he advocates that this “unit of empirical significance” can be an intermediate-sized theoretical package, more than a individual hypothesis or statement (where he agrees with Quine, and Duhem for that matter, that isolated ones cannot be tested alone) but less than the whole contemporary body of scientific knowledge. To see why this is more reasonable, he recalls the predictions about the existence of Neptune by Urbain Le Verrier and John Couch Adams, which certainly did not involve assumptions about bee behavior in the production of honey, as he (perhaps) humorously mentions.
Gillies also shows the relevancy of Duhem’s thesis by illustrating the historical discrepancy between theoretical and observed orbits of Uranus and Mercury. In the first case, the postulation of another planet (Neptune) was correct, whereas for the second case the proposed planet Vulcan was not discovered, and Einstein’s theory was the next step. Both cases show similar observational anomalies, but one led to altering an auxiliary hypothesis (number of planets) and the other to altering a more comprehensive set of statements that comprises a theory.
Underdetermination: Gruesome or Hyperbolized? It seems that a stance that can be adopted and defended by arguments as described above, is one in which “It is rational to hold onto any theory in the face of any evidence.”, as Quine succinctly put it. This notion of underdetermination is misused (and even abused) to justify whatever relativist conclusions one fancies, and to mount attacks against epistemology.
Within Demystifying Underdetermination (1990), Larry Laudan walks us though the trivialities and inconsistencies that were generally employed by his contemporary thinkers when it came to underdetermination. To better understand what follow, it is useful to quickly go over some forms of logic. Although there may only be superficial agreement with regard to the exact taxonomy, one can at least make a simple distinction between deductive and non-deductive logical processes.
For deduction, the conclusions follow logically from the premises, and are true if the premises are considered true. A simple example is if the premises are “All species evolved.” and “Humans are a species.”, then a deductive conclusion is “Therefore, humans evolved.”.
A broad realm of non-deductive reasoning is captured by the term induction, where from a body of data a general statement is inferred that aims to be valid beyond the scope of the observations that support it. It does not establish a certainty, but rather yields statements with a probability of being true (dependent on the nature of the data and the theory of assigning probabilities). Another form of non-deductive logic is abduction, where the “best and most simple” hypothesis (or cause in this case) is inferred from a given observation, as used for example in the board game Mastermind. Again, the conclusion is not a certainty, but simply a suitable one that provides grounds for further orientation and decision-making. The last two, and more generally any non-deductive reasoning, fall under the umbrella term of ampliative logic.
To begin with, Laudan differentiates between two types of underdetermination. Both have sometimes been used as the thesis of underdetermination in the vast literature on the topic. The first, which he calls Humean underdetermination (HUD) amounts to (a variant of) the following claim: “For any finite body of evidence, there are indefinitely many mutually contrary theories, each of which logically entails that evidence.” Although this may sound threatening to science, it is rather weak in two key respects: (i) it is only applicable to deduction and not to the broader class of ampliative logic, and (ii) it doesn’t say that all theories are reconcilable with any given body of evidence, just “indefinitely” many, and it also doesn’t assert that all these rival theories are equally belief-worthy, or equally rational to accept. It simply tells us, that theories (and whether they’re true) cannot be deduced from the phenomena, making deductive reasoning alone insufficient, which all has been increasingly accepted since the time after Newton.
The much stronger thesis to be found, Laudan calls Quinean underdetermination (QUD) and defines it as: “Any theory can be reconciled with any recalcitrant evidence by making suitable adjustments in our other assumptions about nature.” According to this, a theory can be made logically compatible with the refuting evidence, or further be made to function in a logical derivation of the former refuting evidence. However, the crucial concept which all types of underdetermination fall short to address properly is rationality: no such thesis or notion says anything convincing as to whether a theory, which is being saved from refuting evidence, is then still rationally acceptable.
We can suppose that the rational character of a theory could be shown to exist, if the theory (or system it is embedded in) may:
be logically compatible with the evidence; logically entail the evidence; explain the evidence; be empirically supported by the evidence. Although the act of abandoning auxiliary hypotheses of a theory that link to the recalcitrant evidence can trivially satisfy the 1st point, it is by no means guaranteed, that the loss of predictive and explanatory power, as well as empirical support that existed presumably precisely because of these auxiliaries, can be restored easily with alternatives to again satisfy the 2nd, 3rd and 4th points to a sufficient degree.
The true threat to the epistemological project would be ampliative underdetermination in the form of strong egalitarian versions like the QUD. For if these were put into strongly convincing terms, they would, to put it frighteningly, put the flat-earth and the oblate-spheroid hypotheses on equal rational grounds. Kuhn’s version of this would be to hold on to a paradigm come what may. His arguments for this egalitarian claim are, to put it briefly, based on the ambiguous nature of how individuals interpret shared standards. But as we have seen in the previous article, these supposedly deciding factors are rather “unargued dogma” and “if one takes away that dogma, much of the surrounding edifice collapses”, as Laudan now puts it.
A famous example that shows up in such discussions is Nelson Goodman’s grue/green situation. An object is grue only if observed to be green before time $T$, or else it is not observed before time $T$ and is blue. Then, after randomly sampling a pack of emeralds for a while, the hypotheses “all emeralds are green” and “all emeralds are grue” are both equally well supported by our evidence so far, if we pick the time $T$ to lie far in the future. However, and again crucially, whether they are equally belief worthy is usually swept under the rug. One also cannot, as has historically been the case, extrapolate from this example to a global scope and claim the straight rule of inductive inference to never favor a theory unambiguously. In essence, cases where underdetermination may seem relevant (e.g. situations where the number of confirming instances are shared across theories) turn out to be only finely tuned situations of larger, more elaborate wholes (and in Laudan’s words are then “boring trivialities”), where these wholes are meant as the more complex scientific dilemmas in the real world.
The Realm of the Rational Finally, Laudan criticises people that argued for such an egalitarian thesis and claiming underdetermination leading to theory choices being based on “non-logical”, “extra-empirical”, or “social” factors. He wittingly reveals the hidden, and simply untenable assumption that leads to such conclusions, namely that formal logic exhausts the realm of the rational. One needs only to realise the many forms that fall under ampliative logic (and its uses as mentioned throughout this article) to convince oneself that there is more to human rationality than simple formalisable statements.
It is also this binary thinking — everything is either formal logic or sociology — that paints scientists as irrational. It can be found on many occasions throughout history, that scientists (i) changed their mind even in absence of evidence that would seem to force them to, and (ii) clung on to theories even when confronted by (what appeared to be) refuting new evidence. These two facts together haven been misused to argue that scientists can reasonably decide when to change or not change their beliefs, irrespective of what they are coming to learn about the world. However, this would be exactly the same as claiming that, because surgery is not always necessary to cure gall stones, nor always sufficient to cure them, it follows that surgery is never the appropriate treatment of choice for gall stones — a nonsensical conclusion.
The only thing that can be granted to underdetermination postulates is their applicability to logical relations between certain statements. However, they are wholly distinct from, and cannot be used as proof of, any causal interconnections going on in the minds of scientists that presumably (and probably only partially) determine their choices. In Laudan’s words “normative matters of logic and methodology need to be sharply distinguished from empirical questions about the causes of scientific belief.” In other words, the normative underdetermination as perhaps valid to a theory has nothing to say as to whether a scientist’s belief in that theory is causally underdetermined (and vice versa).
For more than a century now, the inquisitive spirit of philosophy has turned its attention to the topic of underdetermination. What gradually became clearer is that the arguments cannot be used to undermine science as a venture, and utterly lack power to lay any claims to the decision-making processes associated to the inner life of scientists. Luckily for humanity(’s scientific enterprise), there seems to exist no firmly established, rationally bolstered underdetermination thesis that has the capacity to seriously put in questions our efforts to develop scientific methodology.
See “Sur les vitesses relatives de la lumière dans l’air et dans l’eau”, Léon Foucault (1853) ↩︎
summary: This article is about part 3 of the anthology Philosophy of Science: Central Issues (1998). This part revolves around the principle of underdetermination, and the related formulations of influential philosophers such as Pierre Duhem and Willard V. O. Quine. In short, underdetermination embodies the idea, that a given body of evidence cannot uniquely determine which theories and beliefs we should espouse. This idea was already mentioned in the previous article about part 2, but will be thoroughly explained in this article.
title: Part 3: The Duhem-Quine Thesis and Underdetermination

contents:
This article is about part 2 of the anthology Philosophy of Science: Central Issues (1998). This part revolves around the seminal work The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) by Thomas Kuhn, as it proposed radical views on how scientists choose between theories. The debate that followed over the next decades revealed many flaws and inconsistencies on his view of the history of science, and included good arguments about the sources of rationality and objectivity in science.
Therefore, this part begins with a “Kuhnian” view on scientific change, and how (according to this view) abrupt and revolutionary changes are its defining characteristics. This view is then discussed and criticised, alternative views that differ in character and intensity being proposed. At the end, discussions about objectivity in science are introduced, as well as the importance of social aspects in science that are highlighted with historic examples.
The Apparent Necessity of Scientific Revolutions According to Kuhn’s historical analysis, the cumulative acquisition of knowledge and the notion that theories build upon previous ones by encompassing them in a larger and “higher” theory proves to be an exception to the rule of scientific development. Rather, a successor theory or paradigm required the dissolution and destruction of a competing or older one and its associated concepts.
Some historic cases supposedly support this idea. One such example concerns the theory of heat. Before Newton’s theory, heat in physical systems was attributed to a substance called the “caloric” that moves across the system from hotter to colder regions. Only with the complete dissolution of these ideas and concepts could we move to the paradigm, where heat was seen equivalent to (mechanical) motion of the constituents of the physical system, i.e. to the theory of thermodynamics. The idea of an additional substance for heat was incommensurable with the idea that heat is, in a way, an emergent quantity.
Another interesting example concerns the idea that Newton’s theory cannot actually be derived from Einstein’s theory. Although we can see Newton’s theory as a set of statements that is a subset of statements of Einstein’s theory, and that apply in the limit $v \ll c$, the physical referents of these Einsteinian concepts are by no means the same as the Newtonian concepts with the same name. Take the concept of mass as an example. Newtonian mass is conserved while Einsteinian is convertible with energy. Only at low speeds can they be measured in similar ways, but still shouldn’t be conceived the same way, as they entail completely different interpretations — one is static, one is transient. Hence, to go from one theory to another, we have to change the fundamental structural elements and their interpretations. Although the mathematical statements of Newton’s theory can be recovered by limiting the statements of Einstein’s theory and changing the meaning of their content, Einstein’s theory can be argued to require the destruction of the ideas of the previous theory to be a successor at all.
As to why revolutionary changes have to take place, Kuhn appeals to the fact that only stubborn anomalies, i.e. those that cannot be reconciled within a current paradigm, lead to new discoveries. The only way forward then, is a radical change to a new paradigm, where these anomalies cease to be stubborn and become explainable.
Kuhn’s Views on Theory Choice We encountered the demarcation question in part 1, that asks where the line between science and pseudoscience lies. A tempting avenue to explore is to enumerate all the values that should guide our debates regarding theory choice. Regarding values and the guiding principles that are supposed to be encapsulated, Kuhn discusses the following five:
Accuracy: deductions and predictions based on theory should be in agreement with experiments and observations, as well as be able to explain them. Consistency: a theory should be free of logical contradictions (internal consistency), and harbour no contradictions with other accepted theories (external consistency). Scope: theoretical consequences should extend beyond the set of questions, observations, and laws the theory was initially designed to explain. Simplicity: a theory should unify isolated phenomena into a larger integrated whole. Fruitfulness: by disclosing new phenomena, a theory should encourage new research. One of the views around his time was, that these criteria provide a shared basis for theory choice between an established paradigm and an upstart competitor. Kuhn argues, that no matter which values you employ, their interpretations vary across individual scientists (even practitioners of the same paradigm) and are too imprecise. They can also conflict with one another, perhaps accuracy favouring the well established theory but scope supporting the visionary competitor. As long as there exists no algorithm to dictate rational, unanimous theory choice — most philosophers belief such an algorithm as unattainable — all relies on subjective factors, idiosyncrasies, and ultimately extrarational choices.
As an example, fruitfulness encapsulates a measure of how promising a theory appears to be in solving puzzles in the future. As this can not be known a priori, Kuhn argues this to require an element of faith that eludes rational evaluation. This was one of Kuhn’s conclusions: subjectivity and touches of irrationality seem to have been the deciding factors in the history of scientific paradigm changes. As the Zeitgeist of the philosophical community involved rational humans doing objective science, his conclusions were received with trepidation.
Kuhn used a few avenues to argue for his views. One is the so-called “Theory-Ladennes of Observation”: What scientists observe depends on the theories they accept, ergo epistemic components provided by observations and experiments alone can’t play the decisive role in theory choice. A simple example to see what is meant by this, and which shows the implausibility of this thesis involves Kepler and Ptolemy watching the sun rise. Kepler sees the sun as stationary, whereas for Ptolemy the sun is a moving planet, so it apparently can’t be the same object they’re observing. But this is a fallacy of equivocation, where the object observed is conflated with the belief that observers have about that object. Another way of seeing it, is that if Ptolemy would be converted to Copernicanism, then he would have the magical power of changing components of the outside world by changing his beliefs.
Another argument is sometimes referred to as “Meaning Variance”: As adherents of different paradigms mean different things when using the same words and phrases, any logical comparison is precluded and paradigms are incommensurable. We experience this in everyday life when we miscommunicate or talk past each other, simply because we hold different connotations to the same words. Meaning related arguments are hard to evaluate, mostly because we have no consensus on what meaning is in the first place. However, what makes Kuhn’s incommensurability claim a non sequitur is that there are more layers to meaning than the one associated to a particular theory and its implicit definitions. For example, a layer of meaning in between that of objects and subjective ideas and conceptualisations about those objects was analysed in On Sense and Reference by Gottlob Frege (1892). The point here being, that some layers may serve as a common ground on which shared meaning can be found across individuals, across paradigms.
Breaking a Paradigm into Pieces Kuhn’s arguments and views have been dissected by many philosophers. Larry Laudan has a particularly comprehensive critique regarding the historical accuracy of Kuhn’s claims, which he laid out in Dissecting the Holist Picture of Scientific Change (1984) (chapter 4 of the linked work). The argumentation convincingly shows that the idea for paradigms to be seen as holistic entities, which one either fully accepts or rejects as a whole, is historically inaccurate and logically unsound.
The concept of a paradigm was used a few times already during this and my previous article about part 1, and it is timely to see the several ways it can be defined.
A paradigm offers a conceptual framework of entities comprising the world and their interactions by making different claims about the nature of those entities and their modes of interaction. A paradigm specifies methods used to inquire about those entities and interactions. A paradigm entails a set of goals, values, and ideals, which its proponents espouse. The claim of Kuhn is that paradigm change requires a simultaneous (rather than sequential or piecemeal) change in all these three categories. He insisted that rationality must be relativised to choices within a paradigm rather than between paradigms, but nothing is offered to make rational choices during interparadigmatic debate still possible. The analogies “conversion experience” and “Gestalt-shift” were used by him for paradigm shifts, which spawned interpretations that invoked religious or irrational aspects. Larry Laudan now shows the view of paradigms as an inextricable, unchangeable mixture of ingredients (such as methods, values, goals, etc.) to be erroneous, because it misses an important part of the dynamics of paradigm shifts: changes within paradigms.
Laudan Loosens the Fit The three definitions above basically describe “levels” that are important for a paradigm: the theoretical, the methodological, and the axiological level. An often used premise in these philosophical discussions, was that these levels form a hierarchy: values and goals assume the top position, influencing the theories and prescribing the employed methods. Ernan McMullin in his Rationality and Paradigm Change in Science (1993) describes certain “lower” values and methods to serve as means to ends, i.e. to attain or satisfy “higher” values and goals of science. Those higher ones are usually set (but debatable on moral grounds), whereas the lower ones justified in an instrumental fashion, their performance evaluated in terms of the goals. If discourse ensues on one level, one uses the concepts of one higher level to argue for a resolution. Naturally, there is a problem if there is disagreement as what permanent attributes of science should comprise the top layer. This is when “conversion experiences” happen.
Laudan now proposes the following. Instead of arranging the components of the three levels in a hierarchy, we reticulate them and suppose that each piece of the net is then negotiable in and of itself. Looking more closely at scientific history, it turns out that this model has high fidelity. The extensive scholarship since Kuhn’s prominent work has shown, that we have collapsed and compressed the indeed gradual changes during scientific revolutions due to our temporal distance, which led to the illusion of abrupt and monumental shifts that happened in a short period. History is actually full of gradual, piecemeal replacements in the reticulational picture. Laudan lists two illustrating examples.
From the time of Francis Bacon (born in the 1560s) until the early 19th century, most scientists subscribed to the rules of inductive inference associated with Bacon, Hume, and Newton, precluding the postulation of any theoretical or hypothetical entities. Newton’s famous phrase “hypotheses non fingo”, that is “to feign (invent) no hypotheses” captures this attitude well. This methodological orientation largely vanished between circa 1800 and 1860, when it was replaced by the logic known as hypothetico-deduction: conjecture a hypothesis and logically deduce what associated observations or empirical work should then be possible. This shift in methods cannot be tied to any shifts in ontology or scientific values of that period. It is well evidenced that, during the 19th century, certainty as the goal of science gave way to producing theories that were plausible, probable, or well tested. From the time of Aristotle onwards, scientists sought theories that were demonstrative and apodictically certain. By the end of the 19th century, most admitted that science could, at most, aspire to highly probable knowledge. This profound epistemic revolution was not specifically associated with the emergence of a new paradigm. On the contrary, fallibilism came to be associated with virtually every major research program, also for the paradigms at odds with each other: atomism and anti-atomism, wave theory and particle theory, Darwinism and Lamarckism, and so on. The axiological shift, independently of the theory and methods employed, was gradually inserted into all paradigms. Contrary to what the holistic picture proclaims, shifts in each level could occur in a largely causally unconnected manner, although they are unquestionable interrelated. Each temporarily fixed point, representing a common ground between paradigms, could therefore be used to hold rational discussions on how to adjust the other nodes in the reticulated scientific enterprise. However, and this has been (and probably still is) debated, even those levels of agreement may sometimes be insufficient to terminate the controversy, which is part of Kuhn’s “subjectivist” thesis. Nevertheless, Laudan soundly argues for the majority of scientific paradigm shifts to have occurred in this piecemeal fashion, and not as a forced “Gestalt-shift” on all levels or in the minds of the scientists.
Fallacies in Underdeterminism A further contribution of Laudan is his critique of the four remaining arguments (the unsoundness of Kuhn’s “Theory-Ladennes of Observation” and “Meaning Variance” arguments were shown above), which Kuhn relied on to make his case for the impotency of methodological rules and shared cognitive values to resolve large-scale scientific disagreement. They support his ideas related to “underdeterminism”, a term which captures when certain construals are insufficient to resolve a certain situation in a clear way.
The “Ambiguity of Shared Standards” Argument.
Kuhn believed that every shared value and principle can be interpreted, judged, and applied differently by different individuals, thus being too ambiguous and imprecise to resolve issues regarding theory choice. The important realisation is that, while indeed some values can indeed be ambiguous at times (like simplicity), many are not. Agreed on their nature by the scientific community, they have been used unambiguously throughout history. For example, consistency of an internal nature, i.e. a non-contradictory structure of a theory, is a matter of logic, proofs, and demonstrations, that are wholly independent of the individuals. Another straightforward example would be novel predictions, which is simply a matter of timely documentation and subsequent juxtaposition of predicted against observed reality. To generalise the ambiguity of one value to all is simply unwarranted.
The “Collective Inconsistency of Rules” Argument.
A similar unjustified extrapolation is done for contradictions arising within a set of shared standards, for example empirical accuracy and generality of a theory. Again, Kuhn argues such disagreements to apply globally to all sets. Laudan identified this erroneous position, and shows that one can find plenty of consistent sets of principles documented and used throughout history, naming “Mill’s methods” first described in A System of Logic by John Stuart Mill (1843) as an example. Many historical examples provide evidence against such extrapolations, and using them to establish a general form for underdetermination becomes illegitimate.
The “Shifting Standards” Argument.
Kuhn’s notion that the holistic paradigms are incommensurable implies that shifts in the standards that govern and define the relevant problems and explanations necessarily accompany paradigm shifts. This argument is addressed by Laudan’s reticulational model of scientific changes, which is far richer and explains historical examples better: disagreements about standards and their preferred methods simply do not have to, and indeed did not, coincide with ontological debates. Laudan finally reiterates the point, that one carries a misunderstanding when claiming that resolutions of disagreements cannot be anything but arbitrary closures, powered by rhetoric rather than rational argument. His reticulational model provides precisely a mechanism by which scientists can identify other shared standpoints even if, say, their standards disagree. Disagreements at the axiological level thus do not demand anything irrational about their resolutions.
The “Problem-Weighting” Argument.
At times, scientists assign different “weights” to different (types of) problems and their (types of) allowed solutions. Thereby, issues that are seen as the most pressing and salient differ, and scientists adhere to the view that only their paradigm can address these issues and provide solutions. Debate about epistemic support of rival paradigms is therefore, Kuhn insists, inevitably inconclusive or that it must be resolved by factors outside rational scientific inquiry. However, the counterargument lies within this argument itself, in the form of a hidden premise: to rationally assign a degree, a “weight” of probative significance to a problem rests on one’s being able to show that there are viable methodological and epistemic grounds that enable such assignments. Exposing these chains of thought and reasoning allows scientists to reflect rationally on their choices, and the same mechanisms used for assigning their degrees in the first place can be used to solve interparadigmatic debate about epistemic significance of problems.
There is another topic of relevance to understand paradigms, which relates to the “Problem-Weighting” argument. Paradigms and their theories have sometimes been devised with a certain “central” problem in mind that needed resolution. However, the centrality of a problem on the paradigms’ explanatory agenda does not necessitate the assignment of a high degree of epistemic or probative weight to that problem when it comes to determining how well supported a certain theory or paradigm is. Historical examples, such as the revolution from “Phlogiston” theory to Dalton’s chemistry entailed a “loss” of explained problems according to the old theory, which did not however make the new paradigm less supported. On the contrary, instances of greatest probative weight in the history of science have not been high on the list of problems that theories were developed to solve. They are precisely the instances that test the theory most “severely”, to use Karl Popper’s words. Some historical examples listed by Laudan, which were generally not high on the list of problems that scientists developed their theories to solve, were the bending of light near the Sun or the recession of Mercury’s perihelion for Einstein’s theory, the Arago disk experiment around Faraday’s times for theories of magnetism, or the reconstitution of white light from the spectrum around Newton’s times for optic theories. What this has to do with paradigm changes, is that Kuhn (and others) have confused the interests of scientists to solve certain problems (the central ones, which motivated the construction of their theories) with the scientist’s judgement concerning how well a paradigm is evidentially supported (via the problems of great probative weight). Conflation of the two can entail the erroneous conclusion, that scientists automatically differ in their epistemic judgements of which theories are well tested, and that irrational means are necessary to resolve their differences.
Objectivity in Science It is commonly believed that science is objective due its impartial and neutral view on nature. This “view from nowhere”, as for example the philosopher Thomas Nagel put it, is supposedly achieved by relying on non-subjective, non-arbitrary criteria for developing, accepting, and rejecting hypotheses and theories that constitute the view. The popular reverence for science is largely based on this belief, but also on the idea that the empirical data used is intrinsically objective. The latter, of course, presupposes that it is accumulated in a robust and honest way, and systematic errors of experiments are understood or non-existent.
Building upon this, the positivist movement within philosophy of science recognised only that which can be scientifically verified or logically (mathematically) proven, rejecting metaphysics and theism, and claiming to be as objective as possible. When asked on how to account for the role of the inevitable subjective aspect in scientific inquiry, the positivists resort to the following contextual distinction.
Context of Discovery.
This context takes care of the subjective influences on the initial formulation of a hypothesis (dreams, intuitive guesses, or other aspects of the mental or emotional life of scientists) but views them strictly as features of an individual’s psychology, standing apart from the scientific process.
Context of Discovery.
In this context, the generative factors associated with the context of discovery are disregarded. The hypothesis is now only considered with respect to its observable consequences that determine its acceptability, purged of any subjective factors, thus rendering scientific inquiries objective.
Adherents of this contextual view isolate subjective influences, effectively treating them as inconsequential quirks of humans and their psyches, and appeal to the objectivity that is intrinsic to the scientific method. To shorten a lengthy discussion and summarise previously encountered arguments, Kuhn points out that this still does not make these intellectual activities objective, because they are carried out in the context of a paradigm. Helen Longino in her work Science as Social Knowledge (1990) investigates the nature and emergence of objectivity in science more carefully, and argues both Kuhn’s view and the contextualist approach to be subject to the same problems. Her key contribution is a shift in perspective: instead of viewing the scientific enterprise as an aggregate of solitary contributions of isolated genius, she enlarges the view until the social web that underlies science becomes visible.
Objectivity by Degrees The history of scientific development may at a glance be perceived as the result of solitary acts of genius. The successful theories appear to have been developed in isolation by a few individuals and their intellectual prowess. Only on closer inspection does survivorship bias reveal itself, and only when accounting for the social structure all these individuals were inevitably embedded in does the emergence of objectivity become clearer. Longino shows how the social aspects of science manifest, to a large degree, in three ways:
Individual scientists are dependent on one another for their practice, as otherwise their ideas cannot proliferate or their sophisticated instruments and experiments cannot be built. Initiation into scientific inquiry requires education, learning traditions, and techniques from individuals having undergone similar initiation and already “living” in the scientific world to be entered. Scientists represent networks embedded in a society, and therefore depend for their survival on that society’s views, specifically whether their work is valued and supported. Social interactions underlie all three. Longino argues objectivity to be, in a way, an emergent property that comes from criticism and peer-review of scientific content. Ideas for theories and experiments are refined by the myriad of minds that comprise the community, and what knowledge may proliferate is essentially decided by these social processes. Most importantly, the questioning of the relevance and function of evidence, as asked by a diverse pool of personalities, can expose the background beliefs, assumptions, and biases that are present within that which is questioned — the theories, experiments, and psyches of individual scientists.
The word dialogue is composed of the Greek words of dia, meaning “through” or “across”, and logos, perhaps translatable to “speech” or “reason”. Monologue can be considered the opposite pole of a continuum. Objectivity, then, arises as the scientific enterprise moves along this continuum from monologue to dialogue. A single perspective of a scientist is transformed into a multifaceted amalgam of views. The intersubjective criticism of the community transforms an initially telescopic view on reality into a kaleidoscopic one. Objectivity of scientific inquiry is thus a consequence of it’s being a social, not an individual, enterprise. There simply exists no objective method that each individual can follow.
To sustain this transformative critical discourse, some criteria have to be met. The existence of platforms for presenting criticism such as journals or conferences is necessary. A list of values can guide scientific criticism. Although they are subject to the weighting problem or the problem of ambiguity as discussed above, it is precisely this open-ended and non-consistent nature of these standards that allows for pluralism and diversity in the sciences. We must realise that such disagreements as seen throughout the history of science are vital to its survival. Lastly, Longino emphasises that sexual and racial asymmetries must also be remedied, as it will increase the diversity of viewpoints, which further increases the degree of objectivity in scientific communities for the reasons outlined above.
Acknowledging Contextual Values A central theme of this article so far has been the changing views on shared values and how they dictate theory choice. The discussions above were about the cognitive values (sometimes also referred to as epistemic values) that concern cognition and knowledge. Naively, we would expect the scientific enterprise to place the value of truth at the top, but in reality most truths have little scientific value (counting hairs on dogs is one example). Although the values discussed above, such as generality or predictive power, are related to truth, they are not reducible to truth in any obvious way. Furthermore, theories cannot be known a priori to be true, so experiments must be performed which then rely on other methods and values themselves. So even if truth were the primary virtue of science, value debates are inevitable, and as argued above, this is a good thing: they help adapt the nature of science and distinguish it from other truth-seeking enterprises such as genealogy, logic, or theology.
Contextual values, on the other hand, are things such as norms, preferences, beliefs, and interests unrelated to the cognitive aims of science. They can be ideological, leading to Nazi Germany rejecting Einstein’s theories because he was Jewish, or take the form of sexual or racial biases. These values depend more strongly on society and culture, vary over time, and can be transformed or rejected without practitioners ceasing to do science.
Some attempts were made to rid the epistemic processes of such contextual values, in a quest to discover the ultimate objective methods for science. One example discussed above was the positivists differentiating between the context of discovery (which they later neglected) and the context of justification (which they appealed to for objectivity). The value-neutrality thesis refers to such a view, where science is free from contextual values, and if there were episodes of “tainted” science in history they were rare. Apart from Helen Longino rejecting this to be an unachievable ideal, Kathleen Okruhlik in her work Gender and the Biological Sciences (1994) makes a simple but strong argument as to why contextual factors inevitably affect the content of science and cannot be exterminated.
The key realisation for her argument lies within a simple characteristic of conjecturing and theorising: when we observe the world and come up with explanations, we compare the resulting hypotheses, in fact, not directly to nature in and of itself, but rather to other rival hypotheses. Therefore, even if we grant the decision procedure between hypotheses to be perfectly objective, if all the hypotheses have been generated, say, in a deeply sexist culture, then all scientific development will be contaminated by sexism, as non-sexist rival hypotheses will never even be generated. The idea that the social influences on scientific development only happen in the context of discovery and get purified in the context of justification does not make sense. And thus the claim that the content of science can be isolated against social influences is erroneous.
Okruhlik shows a few historical examples, where the questions asked and hypotheses generated in the first place were deeply influenced by the biases and asymmetries of the scientific community under consideration. In the biological sciences for example, the initial microscopy perspective on the egg and sperm interactions was completely skewed from the outset due to an androcentric view, which expected the male part to “heroically fight” its way to the passive egg, making the scientists blind to the active role of the female counterpart. As another example, Darwin attributed evolutionary development exclusively to male activity. Anthropological evidence of tool usage and development was interpreted with the “man-the-hunter” story. However, explaining archaeological trends with a gynocentric perspective instead revealed insights into nutritional stress during pregnancy, how mothers fed their young, and how that in turn shaped tool development.
What We Learned There was an idea that the scientific method owes its success to it’s being based on some kind of fundamental laws of discovery, which are intrinsically free from any kind of subjectivity. When practicing these methods one is able to adopt the ultimate “view from nowhere”, allowing to make decisions objectively. In the course of scientific development, philosophers showed this to be an inconceivable quest, devoid of humanity. The arguments presented in this article show but only a glimpse of the debates that ensued, and the wisdom that has been cultivated due to pushing and pulling against such ideas.
The pendulum swung quite far to the opposite side, when Kuhn presented his ideas of the irrationality of scientists to be deciding factors. The society of his time also experienced a descent into postmodernism, where all pretense of objectivity was abandoned and science was portrayed as just another story of the infinite prism of perspectives, any being as good as any other.
Neither of these extremes has fully taken hold of the scientific community at large, however, and works that came later revealed new possibilities of how rationality and objectivity can be reintroduced. One thing so far is clear: humanity and its science form a dynamic relationship, where no participant completely dominates the other. Science is neither irrational, nor can scientific practitioners blindly follow some objective method. It is due to the effort of all of us, and the patiently and compassionately held discussions, that science can progress in a wholesome manner.
